young.html: Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician and inventor. In 1656 his friend Antoine Arnauld was in trouble with the leading teachers of the University of Paris over a hard question about God's grace. Pascal decided to help him in an unusual way: with funny letters.

Pascal pretended to be an ordinary man writing to a friend in the country (“the provinces”), reporting what he heard when he asked learned people to explain the quarrel. They used fancy words that even they could not agree on. Readers laughed, and wanted more.

Then Pascal turned to a bigger target: teachers of his day who, he said, made rules about right and wrong so bendy that almost anything could be excused. He kept writing until there were eighteen letters, printed secretly and passed from hand to hand.

young.name: gb-provincial
young.cap: The eighteen letters, January 1656 to March 1657. Tap one to see what it is about.

young.html: Write a letter that teaches with a smile. Pick a rule you think is silly or confusing (at school, in a game, anywhere). Write a short, polite, funny letter to a friend explaining it by asking innocent questions, the way Pascal did. Remember Pascal's own rule: poke fun at ideas, but be fair to what the other side really says.

full.html: Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) had already made his name in mathematics and physics (see his scientific rung). In 1654 he had a profound religious experience and drew close to the convent of Port-Royal, the center of a movement in the Catholic Church called Jansenism, after the Dutch bishop Cornelius Jansen. The Jansenists stressed, following their reading of Augustine, how much human beings depend on God's grace. Their strongest opponents were many members of the Jesuit order, who emphasized human freedom to cooperate with grace.

In January 1656 the theology faculty of Paris (the Sorbonne) was moving to censure Arnauld, Port-Royal's leading theologian. Pascal answered with an anonymous public letter, then seventeen more, from January 1656 to March 1657. They were collected in 1657 under the name of “Louis de Montalte.”

full.text: We were entirely mistaken. It was only yesterday that I was undeceived. Until that time I had laboured under the impression that the disputes in the Sorbonne were vastly important, and deeply affected the interests of religion.
full.author: Blaise Pascal
full.ed: The Provincial Letters of Blaise Pascal, Robert Carter & Brothers

full.text: Letters I–III: the quarrel over grace

full.html: The narrator visits doctors of the Sorbonne and asks what “proximate power” and “sufficient grace” mean. He finds that the parties who joined to condemn Arnauld agreed on the words but not on what they meant. The joke is that a serious censure rests on a word nobody can define.

full.text: Meanwhile, I leave you at perfect liberty to hold by the word proximate or not, just as you please; for I love you too much to persecute you under that pretext.
full.author: Blaise Pascal
full.ed: The Provincial Letters of Blaise Pascal, Robert Carter & Brothers

full.html: Now the narrator interviews a friendly, talkative Jesuit Father who proudly explains the books of the casuists, writers who work out moral rules for particular cases (from the Latin for “case”). Pascal attacks three ideas in particular as he presents them: probabilism (you may follow any opinion that a single learned author holds, even if the opposite is more likely right), directing the intention (an act can be excused if you fix your mind on a harmless purpose while doing it) and mental reservation (saying something misleading while silently adding words that make it technically true). The Father never notices how his explanations sound.

full.name: gb-provincial
full.cap: Three groups: letters on grace, the dialogues with the Jesuit Father, and the letters addressed to the Jesuits themselves.

full.html: The Jesuits replied, accusing the author of mocking holy things and misquoting. From Letter XI Pascal drops the fictional friend and writes to the Jesuit Fathers directly, defending the use of irony against error and answering their charges point by point. The last two letters, to Father Annat, return to the grace dispute. Letter XVI ends with Pascal's famous apology that the letter is long only because he lacked the leisure to make it shorter.

Why it mattered: the letters showed how clear, witty, everyday French could be used for serious argument. Voltaire, who disagreed with Pascal about religion, called them the first book of genius in French prose.
Taking Pascal's portrait of the casuists as the whole story. It is a brilliant one-sided attack, and its fairness has been argued over ever since; see “Going deeper.”

deep.html: The Jesuits answered that Pascal took quotations out of context, chose the most extreme authors and blamed a whole order for opinions many of its members rejected. Casuistry's defenders say it is a serious attempt to apply moral principles to hard, real cases, as judges and doctors must. Pascal's defenders reply that he quoted accurately and that the opinions he mocked were really being taught. Church authorities acted on both sides: Rome put the Letters on its Index of Forbidden Books in 1657, condemned five propositions attributed to Jansen (1653), and also, in 1665–66 and 1679, condemned a number of lax moral propositions of the kind Pascal had attacked.

Letter XI raises a question every debater meets: is it fair to use laughter in an argument? Pascal says mockery is proper against error but must stay truthful and charitable. Compare Socrates' irony in Plato, Swift and Voltaire in the next era, and Pascal's own Pensées, written in the same years in a very different voice.

items: When is humor a fair way to argue, and when does it become unfair?
Should hard moral cases be decided by rules, by judgment, or both?
Is it right to write anonymously in a public argument?

questions: Pascal made people laugh about a serious quarrel. Do you remember something better when it's funny?
Why might a word that two sides use in different ways cause trouble?
Have you ever heard someone find a “loophole” in a rule? Was it fair?
Pascal said a letter was long because he didn't have time to make it shorter. Why is short writing harder?
How can you disagree with someone strongly and still be fair to what they really believe?
